original_question: For three-dimensional isotropic elastic polycrystals obtained by combining differently oriented grains of a single crystal, what pairs (kappa*,mu*) of effective bulk and shear moduli are achievable? In particular, can one characterize the full feasible region beyond the currently sharp bulk-modulus bounds and the known but non-optimal shear-modulus bounds?
target_in_paper: Section 4, Problem 4.6: "What are the possible (κ∗,μ∗)-pairs for three-dimensional isotropic elastic polycrystals (composites built from a single crystal in various orientations)?"
correct_elements: Your draft already identifies the right object and objective: three-dimensional isotropic elastic polycrystals made from differently oriented grains of a single crystal, described by effective bulk and shear moduli (κ∗, μ∗), and asks for the attainable pair region rather than just a single bound. It also correctly reflects the paper's context that bulk-modulus information is sharper than the corresponding shear-modulus or coupled-pair information.
missing_details: The paper's question is for a fixed underlying three-dimensional single crystal; admissible composites are obtained only by changing grain orientations of that one crystal, not by mixing multiple materials or by passing to the broader class of two-phase isotropic composites.
The word "isotropic" refers to the effective or homogenized response of the polycrystal, so that the effective elasticity tensor is encoded by exactly two scalars, κ∗ and μ∗.
The official formulation asks for the complete set of possible pairs (κ∗, μ∗), not merely for better separate shear bounds once bulk bounds are known.
The status of prior results should be stated precisely: Hill's bounds are optimal for κ∗ in this polycrystal setting.

The shear-modulus nuance is more specific than "known but non-optimal": Hashin-Shtrikman derived improved bounds for μ∗ only under additional assumptions on crystal orientations, and those assumptions are not valid in general.

Nearby context shows that the problem is motivated by the unresolved extremal case of maximizing μ∗ subject to κ∗ = 0, as part of the search for a three-dimensional analogue of the 'ultimate auxetic material'.
No phase-volume-fraction parameter appears here, because all grains are the same material viewed in different orientations.

This is a continuum homogenization problem in three-dimensional linear elasticity; algebraic data such as ambient ring/field, polynomial degree, nilpotency, or quantifiers of the form 'for all sufficiently large m' are not applicable.
refined_question: For a fixed three-dimensional elastic single crystal with given anisotropic elasticity tensor, what is the complete set of pairs (κ∗, μ∗) that can occur as the homogenized effective bulk and shear moduli of macroscopically isotropic polycrystals formed by assembling grains of that crystal in arbitrary orientations? In particular, determine the full attainable region in the (κ∗, μ∗)-plane, including the extremal boundary corresponding to maximal μ∗ when κ∗ = 0.
justification: This draft is targeting Section 4, Problem 4.6 almost verbatim: the paper asks for the possible (κ∗, μ∗)-pairs for three-dimensional isotropic elastic polycrystals built from a single crystal in various orientations. The surrounding discussion explains why this exact formulation is the right one: it is introduced as the three-dimensional barrier in extending the 'ultimate auxetic material' discussion, namely that the polycrystals with largest μ∗ under κ∗ = 0 have not yet been identified. The same paragraph also gives the precise status of known results: Hill's bounds are optimal for κ∗, while generally valid improved bounds for μ∗ or coupled (κ∗, μ∗)-pairs are still lacking, and Hashin-Shtrikman's sharper μ∗ bounds require extra orientation assumptions not valid in general. It should not be broadened to Problem 4.7, which concerns two isotropic elastic phases rather than a polycrystal built from one crystal in varying orientations.
